item.description: Feb 12, 2025; Daytona Beach, Florida, USA; NASCAR Cup Series driver Chris Buescher (17) and NASCAR Cup Series driver Ryan Preece (60) during qualifying for the Daytona 500 at Daytona International Speedway. Mandatory Credit: Peter Casey-Imagn Images NASCAR drivers are known for making some wild bets, but Chris Buescher and Ryan Preece might have come up with one of the funniest punishments imaginable. The two RFK Racing teammates have a wager riding on the final NASCAR Cup Series driver standings. Whoever finishes lower in the points will have to drive 500 laps around a roundabout while the winner gets to sit in the middle and watch the entire thing unfold. Yes, you read that right. Five hundred laps. Around a roundabout. And somehow, that might not even be the funniest part of this story. During media availability at Martinsville Speedway, Preece explained the bet and made it clear that he’d much rather be the one sitting comfortably in the middle, filming his teammate going in circles. “I’d rather be the guy sitting in the center in a chair videotaping him doing it,” Preece joked. He recalled taking part in a jail-and-bail charity event the previous week, where he was calling people in his contacts to help raise money. That’s when it dawned on him that Preece might come up with something that could require actual bail money. Buescher joked that he might need to save some of those contacts for the real thing because he couldn’t ask them for money twice in a matter of weeks without looking like “the Boy Who Cried Wolf.” His comments suggest he’s well aware that Preece could take the punishment to another level. And if you’ve followed these two, you know that wouldn’t be surprising. Earlier this year, Preece pulled a hilarious prank on Buescher by arranging billboards near Atlanta Motor Speedway. One featured Buescher wearing a wig and shawl with the message, “Come see me race this weekend!” Another poked fun at Buescher’s Texas hometown by directing people to Prosper, Texas. Buescher made it clear at the time that payback was coming. Now, with the roundabout bet hanging over them, he might have the perfect opportunity to get even. item.description: Glazers reportedly possess ability to force Ratcliffe sale of Man United as owners furious with 'downgrade' originally appeared on The Sporting News . Add The Sporting News as a Preferred Source by clicking here . Things have been chaotic at Manchester United this season to say the least, as the Red Devils are on a catastrophic winless run which has not only put manager Michael Carrick under fire, but also the ownership group. United lost 2-0 to Chelsea on Saturday, the club's second straight Premier League defeat which left them without a victory on the domestic season since August 30 when they beat newly-promoted Ipswich Town . They have failed to win any of their last nine games across all competitions, dating back to a 4-0 victory over Champions League minnows Sabah on September 10. With United sitting 17th in the top flight table, it marks their worst start to any league season in the Premier League era through their first eight games, with just seven points through their first nine games. The current situation leaves the fans irate with how far United have fallen under current ownership, with both the Glazer family and Jim Ratcliffe in their sights. MORE: All the latest Man United news Glazer family can reportedly force Ratcliffe sale of Man United Despite taking a back seat in terms of the day-to-day football operations, the Glazers remain as majority owners of Manchester United, in control of 72% of the club's shares. When Jim Ratcliffe bought 28% of the club in early 2024, the INEOS chief assumed operational control of the club per the terms of their deal. According to multiple reports in England, including ESPN , the minority sale to Ratcliffe includes a "drag-along" clause that would force Ratcliffe to sell his 28% share of the club if the Glazers wished to sell, pushing through a 100% sale, effectively forcing Ratcliffe to offload his portion whether he wants to or not. The ESPN report states that if a sale is procured before February 2027, Ratcliffe is guaranteed $33 per share, which is what he purchased his ownership stake for, but once that clause expires, the Glazers can sell for any figure whether Ratcliffe is happy with the price or not. As of close of business on Friday, October 23, Man United share price sat at $20.61. The ESPN report claims that the Glazer family does want to sell, but that they are "waiting for the right time to cash in," saying there is "no market right now for investors looking to buy a Premier League team," partly because of issues with United particularly, and partly because of outside forces, such as the pending Manchester City punishment. item.description: Ohio State Buckeyes defensive lineman Robert Landers (67) tackles USC Trojans running back Ronald Jones II (25) during the third quarter of the Goodyear Cotton Bowl Classic at AT&T Stadium in Arlington, Texas on Dec. 29, 2017. This result shook up the national landscape just days before the SEC power rankings for Week 10 were released on Sunday, Nov. 1. While the Buckeyes suffered their second loss of the season, the teams in the Southeast are moving forward with strong momentum. The defense played a significant role by stopping Florida’s offense before it could build any real momentum. The Gators were so ineffective that they were forced to make a quarterback change late in the game. This level of control is exactly what a national championship team needs to show on the biggest stages. item.description: MINNEAPOLIS, MN - OCTOBER 25: Minnesota Vikings wide receiver Jauan Jennings (14) runs off the field after a NFL game between the Indianapolis Colts and the Minnesota Vikings on October 25, 2026 at U.S. Bank Stadium in Minneapolis, MN. (Photo by Jeffrey Brown/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images) | Icon Sportswire via Getty Images The NFL’s trade deadline is rapidly approaching, and the Minnesota Vikings reportedly had a deal in place for a player who has been underperforming this season, but the trade fell through. The #49ers and #Vikings recently had a trade agreement in place for WR Jauan Jennings to return to San Francisco, but Jennings made it clear he didn’t want to go back, and the deal fell through, per @JayGlazer . pic.twitter.com/aqCgTn5l0M — Ari Meirov (@MySportsUpdate) November 1, 2026 Per Jay Glazer of FOX Sports (via Air Meirov of The 33rd Team), the Vikings had a deal in place to send wide receiver Jauan Jennings. . .who has been the subject of recent trade rumors, back to the San Francisco 49ers, but the deal fell through when Jennings made it clear that he did not want to go back to San Francisco. Jennings spent the first six seasons of his NFL career with the Niners after they selected him in the seventh round of the 2020 NFL Draft out of Tennessee. During his time in San Francisco, he caught 210 passes for 2,584 yards and 22 touchdowns. He signed a 1-year deal with Minnesota this offseason, and thus far, he has been a significant disappointment, catching just four passes for 43 yards. No word has been given on why Jennings did not want to go back to San Francisco or anything like that. . .just that he didn’t want to go back to his former team. At this point, it’s not clear if Jennings would be open to a trade to any other team or if he just didn’t want to go back to San Francisco. The NFL trade deadline is a week from this coming Tuesday. We’ll be keeping an eye on what the Vikings are doing and whether or not they make any moves for the stretch run of the 2026 NFL season.

item.title: ‘Replay was incorrect’: Big 12 admits officiating mistake that resulted in touchdown
item.description: Sep 19, 2026; College Park, Maryland, USA; The referee checks the instant reply on Maryland Terrapins touchdown in the first half against the Virginia Tech Hokies at SECU Stadium. Mandatory Credit: Jamie Sabau-Imagn Images BYU has found itself in the middle of yet another officiating controversy, and the Big 12 has now admitted that it got the call wrong. The Big 12 acknowledged after Saturday’s game that replay officials incorrectly awarded the No. 8 Cougars a first-quarter touchdown in their 27-20 win over Arizona State. It marks the third straight week that a BYU game has featured questionable officiating. A Pattern of Controversy BYU has been involved in a string of close games with controversial finishes. After the Cougars’ 28-24 win over Notre Dame on Oct. 17, the Big 12 said that one more second should have been put back on the clock , which would have given the Fighting Irish a chance at one final play. The following week, BYU lost 39-31 in double overtime at UCF. That game went to overtime after BYU blocked a 47-yard field goal attempt on third down. UCF kicker Will Stone recovered the ball and would have had a chance to try another game-winning kick. But officials ruled that Stone’s helmet came off during the play, triggering a 10-second runoff that ended regulation. ‘Replay Was Incorrect’ On Saturday, the controversy came on BYU’s first possession. On second-and-goal from the 1-yard line, quarterback Bear Bachmeier fumbled while running up the middle, and running back Sione Moa picked up the ball and ran it in for a touchdown, according to ESPN’s Max Olson . Officials initially blew the play dead and ruled that Bachmeier was stopped short. After reviewing it, they determined that he fumbled and that BYU recovered. A second review by the Big 12’s replay operations center in Irving, Texas, then overturned the play to a touchdown. But according to the rulebook, any advance after a fumble recovery in that situation is nullified. The Big 12 admitted the mistake in a statement after the game. “Replay was incorrect in awarding a score,” the Big 12 said. “The correct ruling should have been BYU ball for a third-and-goal from the 2-yard line.” ‘That’s All Back Home’ Arizona State head coach Kenny Dillingham argued with officials at the time, and he voiced his frustration after the loss. “I was trying to argue that he does have the right to recover it post-whistle, but that’s not a clear advancement, which means the ball should be at the 3,” Dillingham said, via ESPN . Dillingham made it clear that he didn’t blame the officials on the field. “Obviously, that wasn’t what happened. It’s not the officials’ fault. Those officials don’t have say in that. That’s all back home,” Dillingham said. BYU would have still had a chance to score from the 2-yard line. But in a seven-point game, Arizona State fans will surely be wondering what could have been.
